Deux pliants ultra-fins, mais pas aussi rassurants
Ouverts, les deux ressemblent à de petites tablettes : 4,1 mm d’épaisseur pour le Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, 4 mm pour le Magic V6. Le modèle de Samsung est toutefois plus léger avec 215 g contre 224 g. Sa charnière paraît solide, sa pliure est très discrète et son châssis mêle aluminium, verre renforcé et titane. Son bloc photo le fait en revanche trembler sur une table.
Le nouveau pliant de Honor est plus stable et surtout mieux protégé. Sa certification IP68/69 couvre poussière, immersion et jets d’eau, loin devant l’IP48 du Fold 8 Ultra. La firme chinois le rend également compatible avec un stylet vendu séparément, alors que Samsung abandonne le S Pen. Tous deux proposent 5G, NFC, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 et lecteur d’empreintes latéral.
Samsung éblouit, Honor affiche des couleurs plus justes
Côté affichage, tous deux utilisent des écrans Amoled LTPO (jusqu’à 120 Hz. Le Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra dispose d’un cover display de 6,5 pouces et 8 pouces à l’intérieur ; le Magic V6, 6,52 et 7,95 pouces. Le sud-coréen domine nettement en luminosité avec environ 2880 cd/m² sur ses deux dalles, contre 2043 cd/m² à l’extérieur et 1325 cd/m² à l’intérieur chez Honor.
Le V6 se rattrape avec un antireflet remarquable et des couleurs presque parfaites une fois le bon mode activé. Samsung reste excellent en plein soleil et réduit lui aussi fortement les reflets sur son grand écran, mais son réglage le plus fidèle réchauffe un peu trop l’image.
Même puissance, énorme différence de température
Nos deux duellistes embarquent une puce Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 et font tourner sans peine plusieurs apps en même temps ou des jeux exigeants. La vraie différence apparaît avec la chaleur : le modèle de Samsung reste autour de 42°C sous forte charge, quand le pliant signé Honor a atteint 54°C avant de se mettre en sécurité.
Côté logiciel, le Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra tourne sous Android 17 avec One UI 9, et bénéficie de sept ans de support logiciel. Le Magic V6 reste sous Android 16, avec sept ans de mises à jour également, beaucoup d’outils d’IA et une prise en charge des AirPods, AirDrop et des notifications Apple. Il arrive cependant avec trop d’applications préinstallées.
Photo et autonomie : Honor sort les gros chiffres
Samsung réunit un capteur principal de 200 Mpx, un ultra grand-angle de 50 Mpx et un zoom optique x3 de 10 Mpx. De jour, ses photos sont détaillées, naturelles et bien exposées. L’ultra grand-angle convainc aussi, mais le zoom perd beaucoup de précision la nuit. Les deux caméras selfie de 10 Mpx sont correctes et la vidéo monte jusqu’en 8K à 30 i/s.
Honor joue davantage la régularité avec 50 Mpx pour le module principal et l’ultra grand-angle, puis 64 Mpx pour le zoom x3. Les couleurs sont plus vives et son téléobjectif conserve davantage de détails dans l’obscurité. Les deux capteurs selfie atteignent 20 Mpx et la vidéo arrière culmine en 4K 60 i/s.
Samsung adopte enfin le silicium-carbone pour sa batterie de 5000 mAh : 21 h 27 min d’autonomie moyenne et 56 min pour une charge complète à 45 W. Honor propose une capacité encore plus généreuse de 6660 mAh et tient en moyenne 22 h 21 min. Le V6 supporte une charge 80 W en filaire et 66 W sans-fil, mais demande tout de même 1 h 24 min pour faire le plein.
On fait le bilan, calmement
Ces deux smartphones pliants haut de gamme méritent amplement leurs 5 étoiles. Le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra est le plus équilibré : plus léger, beaucoup plus lumineux, particulièrement à l’aise en multitâche et peu sujet aux montées de fièvre. Son étanchéité limitée, l’absence de stylet et ses photos de nuit au téléobjectif restent cependant ses principales faiblesses.
Le Honor Magic V6, lui, met le paquet sur l’équipement avec sa batterie XXL, sa protection IP68/69, et la constance de son volet photo. En revanche, sa chauffe importante sous forte sollicitation est son vrai point noir. À prix voisin, Samsung privilégie donc le confort et la maîtrise, tandis que Honor mise sur l’autonomie et l’équipement. Vous voilà prévenus.

articles.title: La mayor amenaza medieval para el Papa nació en un remoto pueblo aragonés. Gobernó desde Peñíscola hasta que lo envenenaron
articles.text:
En el año 2000, un cráneo parcialmente momificado apareció en un palacio de Sabiñán, en Zaragoza. Los análisis lo identificaron como los restos de un papa del siglo XV. Alguien lo había robado de la urna donde reposaba. La Guardia Civil lo recuperó meses después, el 12 de septiembre. El cráneo lleva décadas generando un pleito judicial entre tres localidades —Illueca, Sabiñán y Peñíscola— que reclaman su custodia. Hoy descansa en un depósito del Museo Provincial de Zaragoza, esperando sentencia —lo contamos hace un año—. Siglos antes, un santo le había profetizado ese destino: con su cabeza jugarán los niños a modo de pelota. La historia de cómo acabó así empieza en un castillo del Moncayo.
Desafiando a toda la cristiandad. Pedro Martínez de Luna y Pérez de Gotor. Segundo hijo varón de una de las familias nobles más poderosas de Aragón. El primogénito heredaba el feudo; el segundo iba a la Iglesia. Era la costumbre. Pedro de Luna estudió Derecho Canónico en la Universidad de Montpellier —donde destacó como alumno y después como profesor— y fue nombrado cardenal por el papa Gregorio XI. En 1377, la monja dominica Catalina de Siena recordó al papa una promesa de juventud: devolver la sede a Roma. Gregorio XI, conmovido, regresó. Pedro de Luna viajó con él. Lo que viene a continuación, como dice el meme, te sorprenderá, porque partió la Iglesia en dos durante cuarenta años.
Gregorio XI murió en Roma el 27 de marzo de 1378 antes de poder reorganizarse. El cónclave que eligió a su sucesor fue un caos: la turba romana rodeó el edificio exigiendo un papa italiano bajo amenaza de muerte. El resultado fue Urbano VI, el arzobispo de Bari. Meses después, los cardenales —Pedro de Luna entre ellos— declararon inválida esa elección por coacciones y eligieron a Roberto de Ginebra, que tomó el nombre de Clemente VII y se instaló en Aviñón. La Iglesia tenía dos papas. Ambos se excomulgaron mutuamente y ambos maldijeron a los seguidores del otro. Nadie sabía con certeza cuál de los dos iba al infierno. Esto último no es un chiste.
Cómo llega Pedro de Luna al pontificado. Por una mezcla de mérito, oportunismo y una promesa que pensaba saltarse. Durante dieciséis años fue el legado del papa de Aviñón en toda Europa. Medió entre Portugal y Castilla. Negoció entre Francia e Inglaterra, enfrentadas en la Guerra de los Cien Años. Era una de las figuras que mejor conocía el mapa político y jurídico de la cristiandad. Cuando Clemente VII murió en septiembre de 1394, los cardenales de Aviñón se encontraron ante un problema: elegir un nuevo papa perpetuaba el Cisma —de ahí la palabra—. Lo denominaron via cessionis: que ambos papas renunciasen para cerrar el Cisma.
Los doctores de París aconsejaron esperar. Todos los cardenales firmaron una cédula comprometiéndose a renunciar al pontificado si eran elegidos. Era la condición para aceptar el cónclave. El lunes siguiente, 20 de 21 cardenales votaron a Pedro de Luna. El único que no lo hizo fue él mismo. Aceptó el cargo. Tomó el nombre de Benedicto XIII. Y no renunció. Cuando le preguntaron por el juramento, respondió con la lógica de un jurista: ningún cardenal puede comprometerse a renunciar antes de ser elegido, porque eso violaría la libertad del Espíritu Santo. El juramento era inválido de raíz. Nadie lo convenció de lo contrario en los siguientes veintinueve años.
Legitimando, que es gerundio. Aragón, Castilla, Navarra y Escocia lo consideraron su santo Papa. Todos los demás, no. Eso son cuatro reinos contra el resto de la cristiandad. Francia, que había sido el principal sostén del papado de Aviñón, le retiró la obediencia en 1398. En 1403 abandonó el Palacio de los Papas de Aviñón con solo cinco cardenales fieles. Esto implica mover ejércitos y embajadas. Deambuló por ciudades de Francia e Italia mientras negociaba, maniobraba y publicaba tratados jurídicos. Era el papa más solo de la historia. Y el más obstinado.
Perpiñán, 1415. Ahora llega el momento más cinematográfico. El Concilio de Constanza, convocado por el emperador Segismundo, conseguía lo que ninguno había logrado: el antipapa Juan XXIII fue depuesto, y Gregorio XII, el papa romano, renunció en favor de la unificación. Solo quedaba Benedicto XIII. En septiembre de 1415, el mismísimo Vicente Ferrer —su amigo de décadas, predicador de fama europea, futuro santo— viajó a Perpiñán para convencerle. No lo logró. Se topó con este argumento: “Aseguráis que soy un papa dudoso; lo acepto. Pero antes de ser papa fui cardenal, y cardenal indiscutible de la Santa Iglesia de Dios, ya que fui investido antes del Cisma. Como los cardenales son quienes nombran al papa, solo yo puedo designar o elegir un papa auténtico”.
Vicente Ferrer lo dejó ahí, encerrado en ese círculo vicioso. Fernando I de Aragón lo abandonó también. El Concilio de Constanza lo condenó como hereje y antipapa. Martín V fue nombrado pontífice único de la cristiandad en 1417. Pedro de Luna, más solo que la una, se instaló en el castillo templario de Peñíscola.
Qué pasa, Peñíscola. La última roca era su creación más personal. El castillo de Peñíscola, sobre un promontorio frente al Mediterráneo, fue el teatro de los últimos ocho años de su vida. Allí construyó una corte y creó una de las bibliotecas más ricas del siglo XV, con volúmenes de teología, filosofía, arquitectura, medicina, alquimia, astrología y magia. Los “libros ocultos” de su colección le valieron acusaciones de hechicería y cultos demoníacos. Se decía que en su poder estaba el legendario Códice Imperial, un pergamino escrito por el propio Constantino cuya lectura helaba la sangre (y sacudía la fe). Guardado en una cánula de oro, era el secreto mejor custodiado de la Iglesia. Cuando Benedicto murió, nadie lo encontró.
En 1418, con 90 años, lo envenenaron con rejalgar, una mezcla de arsénico y azufre. El atentado lo organizó un cardenal al servicio de Martín V. Un médico hebreo lo trató con un compuesto que desde entonces se llamó "Pulveris Papae Benedicti". Pues, ¿sabes qué? Sobrevivió. Rodeado por tropas aragonesas, con el mundo entero reconociendo a otro papa, siguió gobernando desde el peñón. Siguió nombrando cardenales, y siguió firmando bulas. Murió el 23 de mayo de 1423. Tenía entre 94 y 95 años. Sus últimas palabras: "Papa sum". Un maquinarias.
Y después vino la profecía. Porque la profecía de Vicente Ferrer empezó a cumplirse. Sus restos fueron embalsamados y permanecieron en Peñíscola durante 7 años, venerados por el pueblo como si fuera un santo. En 1430 los trasladaron a Illueca, su pueblo natal. Allí reposaron en una urna de cristal y madera, custodiados por la familia Luna. Un extranjero italiano destrozó la urna intentando profanarlos… y el arzobispo de Zaragoza tapió la sala para protegerlos.
Siglos después, durante las guerras napoleónicas, soldados franceses saquearon el castillo de Illueca. Golpearon la momia. Arrojaron los huesos al río Iruela. Antes, dejaron que unos niños jugaran con el cráneo. Labradores que trabajaban río abajo reconocieron el cráneo flotando y lo devolvieron a la familia Luna. Los demás huesos se perdieron para siempre. El cráneo pasó al palacio del Conde de Argillo en Sabiñán. La expresión “mantenerse en sus trece” probablemente le debe algo, por aquella insistencia en repetir “Papa sum et XIII” en su retiro a Peñíscola. El antipapa para los otros no cedió en su postura durante casi tres décadas. Un canonista más papista que los papas, empapado de su propia bula (papal).

articles.title: Jeff Bezos compra una parte del Liverpool: cuál será su papel en el equipo de la Premier League
articles.text:
Jeff Bezos llega al fútbol al hacer parte de un consorcio de inversores que adquirió el 30% del Liverpool.
El acuerdo fue anunciado oficialmente tras la firma de un “acuerdo definitivo” entre el propietario del club, Fenway Sports Group (FSG), y el consorcio inversor conocido como 1892 Holdings. Este grupo no solo incluye a Bezos, sino también a figuras como Eduardo Saverin, cofundador de Facebook, el empresario británico-indio Amit Bhatia y la familia Mittal, conocida mundialmente por su emporio siderúrgico.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo es la operación en la que Jeff Bezos invierte en el Liverpool
El consorcio liderado por Bhatia acordó adquirir aproximadamente el 30 % de las acciones del Liverpool FC, según comunicaron fuentes del club y agencias como EFE. El valor total de la operación se sitúa en torno a 2 mil millones de dólares, lo que equivale a una valoración global del club cercana a los 7 mil millones de dólares.
1892 Holdings está integrado por varios pesos pesados del mundo empresarial. Además de Bezos y Saverin, destacan los fideicomisos de la familia Mittal, el fondo K5 Sports (de K5 Global, con Bezos como inversor principal) y EE Capital, la oficina familiar de Elaine y Eduardo Saverin.
PUBLICIDAD
Amit Bhatia, quien fue copropietario del Queens Park Rangers durante casi dos décadas, asumirá la vicepresidencia del club, mientras que Bryan Baum y Elaine Saverin se incorporarán al consejo directivo.
Según el comunicado oficial, la transacción está sujeta a las aprobaciones regulatorias correspondientes y a condiciones habituales de cierre. FSG, por su parte, mantendrá la participación mayoritaria y el control operativo del club, aunque el acuerdo otorga al consorcio opciones para aumentar su participación si el grupo estadounidense decide vender en el futuro.
PUBLICIDAD
La llegada de estos inversores representa una apuesta por la proyección internacional de la marca Liverpool y la generación de nuevas fuentes de ingresos comerciales. En palabras de Amit Bhatia, la decisión de invertir responde a la profunda confianza en el liderazgo del club y la voluntad de apoyar el éxito continuado de la entidad en los próximos años.
Cuáles son las implicancias financieras y regulaciones de la Premier League
A pesar de la magnitud de la inversión, la entrada de Bezos y su consorcio no se traducirá en un aumento inmediato del presupuesto para fichajes. La Premier League cuenta con regulaciones estrictas destinadas a mantener la sustentabilidad financiera y la paridad competitiva entre los clubes.
PUBLICIDAD
Las normas establecen que el gasto en plantilla no puede superar el 85 % de los ingresos futbolísticos y las ganancias netas por venta de jugadores.
Por lo tanto, aunque Liverpool cuente ahora con tres de los empresarios más ricos del planeta entre sus accionistas, el club no podrá gastar sin límites en el próximo mercado de transferencias. El impacto inmediato se orienta a fortalecer la posición financiera y a potenciar la estrategia comercial global, más que a realizar inversiones masivas en refuerzos deportivos.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuál es el secreto de Jeff Bezos cuando se siente estresado
Jeff Bezos, fundador de Amazon, reveló su estrategia para manejar el estrés: actuar de inmediato sobre la causa. Según él, el estrés es una señal de que algo requiere atención.
En una charla, explicó que en vez de buscar relajarse, prefiere identificar el origen de la ansiedad y dar el primer paso para resolver el problema. Además, suele transformar el reto en un trabajo colectivo, buscando aliados y soluciones creativas. Para Bezos, enfrentar el conflicto reduce la ansiedad y convierte la preocupación en un proceso estimulante.
PUBLICIDAD
Especialistas como la Clínica Mayo también sugieren hábitos saludables, actividad física y apoyo profesional si el estrés se vuelve difícil de manejar o interfiere con la vida cotidiana.

articles.title: ‘Smoother than an olympic diver slathered in goose fat’ — the affordable OnePlus Nord CE5 seriously impressed me with its slick performance and fluid 120Hz display
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Given its affordable price, using the OnePlus Nord CE5 is a surprisingly polished experience. Both its display and camera deliver seriously dynamic color, its OS is smooth to use and makes multitasking a breeze, and its battery can outlast many flagship phones. Admittedly, its chipset is far from top of the range, it’s packed with more bloat than I’d like, and it can’t handle games on max graphics settings, but none of its shortcomings are egregious. It’s a seriously skilled phone in many areas given its low price tag.
Pros
- +Vibrant display
- +Great productivity performance and gesture control
- +Rich, colorful photography
- +Epic 20-hour battery life
Cons
- -Middling chipset
- -Too much bloat
- -Limited to 2x optical zoom
Why you can trust TechRadar
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: two-minute review
The OnePlus Nord CE5 is an affordable yet premium-feeling handset that punches way above its weight. Although its successor, the CE6, has launched in some markets, OnePlus has confirmed that it and future handsets will no longer sell in the UK. So, in lieu of a newer version, is the CE5 still worth your consideration?
The OnePlus Nord CE5’s design certainly doesn’t make it look bargain basement, but it doesn’t feel super luxe either. While it’s pleasantly tactile under your fingertips, there’s no confusing its plastic edges for metal, and I’m not totally bowled over by the pearlescent effect on the Marble Mist colorway. However, I will grant that it feels solidly made and its vertical camera module looks pretty neat when so many handsets’ lenses look like they’ve been grafted on by Dr. Frankenstein.
Although it’s not a total knockout, the Nord CE5’s display definitely packs a punch given its price. Colors are bold and vivid, making the nature documentaries I was watching seriously pop. Its 387PPI display showed off most images in crisp detail, even if it wasn’t as pin sharp as some of the best phones. On the flip side, whites run a little bit blue for my liking, and the display is not quite bright enough to make up for how reflective its screen is. Still, there was plenty about the screen that dazzled me, figuratively at least.
Under the hood, the Nord CE5 runs the MediaTek Dimensity 8350 Apex chipset. That’s not a current-gen SoC by any means, but I still got great productivity performance out of it. Not only was I able to have myriad apps open, but I also ran Google Docs and a streaming app in split-screen with no noticeable slowdown.
Gaming performance was also pretty stable. Playing lengthy sessions of both Call of Duty: Mobile and Genshin Impact, the Nord CE5 ran very smoothly and showed no hint of lag or jitter. Cranking the graphics settings up to their highest on Genshin Impact did throw up a warning that I was overclocking the CPU, though, so while performance remained stable, you might not want to run things that high. On the plus side, the Nord CE5 didn’t experience all that much warming during this, thanks to its CryoVelocity graphene vapor chamber.
Based on Android 15, the OxygenOS 15.0 that the Nord CE5 runs on is nice and agile. Multitasking is easy thanks to its split-screen mode and there are great shortcuts on offer, like screen-off gestures that let you open the camera or switch on the flashlight by tracing an O or V on the display. On the whole, its AI tools are unobtrusive yet helpful, and OnePlus offers a full six years of software updates. The only thing I don’t love here is the bloat that comes pre-installed — seriously, phone makers, can you stop foisting Temu on me?
For a phone in this price range, the Nord CE5 also offers a very decent camera. Whether I was popping off shots of brilliant yellow roses or the deep blue sky reflected in a river, colors felt vibrant and its HDR performance rendered textures like stonework with a nice depth. Admittedly, its smaller 1/1.95 inch sensor can’t quite rival flagship phones in terms of sheer detail, but it still captured textures and details with real precision. And even though I’d personally prefer at least a 3x lens in my camera, the 2x zoom conveyed excellent detail without showing any distortions or aberrations.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
In my book, though, by far the Nord CE5’s strongest feature is its battery. OnePlus has managed to eke more than 20 hours of life out of its 5,200mAh battery, meaning it can happily outlast many of the flagship phones we’ve reviewed in recent times. Not only that, but during my testing I found its 80W SUPERVOOC charging could comfortably juice it up from 0% to 100% in just 59 minutes, which is blisteringly fast.
All in all, the Nord CE5 is a solid, if unexceptional, phone… until you consider its price point. Considering a list price that starts at £299, there are many areas it pulls ahead of similarly priced rivals, while in some areas — chiefly battery life — it can honestly give flagships a run for their money. Ultimately, if your intended spend sits on the border between budget and mid-range phone, the Nord CE5 has plenty of highlights and few enough deficits to make it a worthy investment.

OnePlus Nord CE5 review: Price and availability
- Launched on July 8, 2025
- List price of £299 for 128GB storage or £349 for 256GB
- Succeeded by the Nord CE6 — but that’s not available in the UK
Having launched on July 8, 2025, the OnePlus Nord CE5 is currently available in the UK. While it has technically been supplanted by the OnePlus Nord CE6, released on May 8, 2026, the latter isn't sold in the UK and, with no launch rumored, is unlikely to make it here at all. So that means the Nord CE5 is still the budget OnePlus to aim for if you’re a Brit.
When it comes to cost, the Nord CE5 retails for a list price of £299 for the model with 128GB of storage or £349 for 256GB. That means it leans slightly more toward budget territory than mid-range. You can choose from one of two colorways for that spend, either the minimal Black Infinity version or the iridescent Marble Mist I’ve tested here.
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: design
- Solid, robust-feeling design
- Easy to hold one-handed
- Personally not keen on marble colorway
Overall, I like the build of the OnePlus Nord CE5. While it doesn’t quite feel as premium as more expensive phones — that lightweight plastic trim around its edge can’t compete with my iPhone 16 Pro’s titanium, for example — that flat design still feels comfortable in your hand.
Measuring 6.44 x 2.99 inches / 163.58 x 76.02mm, the Nord CE5 is slightly taller and less broad than some of its affordable rivals, making it easy to hold in one hand — although you might need your second hand to reach the very top of the screen. But, at 0.33 inches / 8.27mm, and 0.32 inches / 8.17mm deep for the Marble Mist / Black Infinity versions respectively, it’s not the thinnest device on the market, with only a few handsets like the Nothing Phone (4a), iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max being thicker.
As I’ve mentioned above, the Nord CE5 comes in two colorways: Black Infinity and Marble Mist. Honestly, I’m not a huge fan of the pearlescent marble effect — while it sounds premium, in reality it looks a touch gaudy to me. On the plus side, its matte finish feels wonderfully smooth, with just enough of a grain to remain tactile.
Perhaps unsurprisingly given the budget price, its design is pretty minimal elsewhere. But that’s actually something of a relief, given how crowded some flagship phones can now feel with their full-width camera modules and bunches of bonus buttons. The Nord CE5’s vertically aligned dual-lens camera module looks neat and nicely self-contained, while it only has a lock button and volume rocker adorning one edge, making it feel lean and sparing.
- Design score: 3.5 / 5
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: display
- Vibrant, satisfying colors
- Solid resolution, albeit not flagship sharp
- Lacking in brightness
Measuring 6.77 inches, the OnePlus Nord CE5’s screen is more expansive than that of many flagships. It outstrips the iPhone 17 Pro and Samsung Galaxy 26+ at 6.3 and 6.7 inches respectively, although it’s not quite as extensive as phones like the 6.83-inch Nothing Phone (4a) Pro or the 6.9-inch iPhone 17 Pro Max and Samsung Galaxy 26 Ultra.
OnePlus has shared 2392 x 1080 pixels across that display, giving the Nord CE5 a pixel density of 387PPI. Keen to see how that stacks up in practice, I streamed Planet Earth II in 1080p on the Nord CE5 side-by-side with my 460PPI iPhone 16 Pro. During a scene involving a pride of lionesses on the savannah grappling with an African buffalo, the Nord CE5 felt just a tiny bit less crisp, with the drops and spray of water being cast up not feeling quite as sharp as on my premium phone. Most images still look pretty crisp though, even if they’re not quite up to flagship standard.
On paper, the OnePlus Nord CE5 offers 1430 nits peak brightness and a typical brightness of 800 nits. Unfortunately, its display didn’t exactly feel dazzlingly bright to me. Some scenes felt like their white level was a bit too low; for example, the canopy of a jungle looked thicker and more oppressive than it did on other screens. And the whites that are there are a little too cold for my liking, with the white highlights of exposed tree bark looking a little on the blue side.
This isn’t helped by the fact that the Nord CE5’s display is quite reflective. While most phones reflect the lighting in the TechRadar testing labs — they're huge fluorescent ceiling panels — the OnePlus’s display seems to mirror many other objects in the room as well. Without the extra brightness that more expensive models are capable of, it can’t quite overcome local sources of light.
That’s a shame because the Nord CE5’s color fidelity is pretty spot on elsewhere. Watching a Wilson’s bird of paradise trying to court a mate, I was impressed with how vibrantly the display rendered its bright blue crown, red back and yellow mantle, not to mention its bright green fluorescent collar. But thanks to that slight paucity of white highlights, it still doesn’t have quite the HDR pop it otherwise could have.
I’ll give the Nord CE5 credit where it’s due though: the display’s max 120Hz refresh rate ensures that everything looks smoother than an Olympic diver slathered in goose fat. Navigating menus and swiping between apps, everything felt wonderfully fluid and never showed even a hint of judder or slowdown. The device can absolutely rival any premium handset here.
- Display score: 3.5 / 5
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: Software
- Great gestures and shortcuts built in
- Unobtrusive AI tools
- Quite a lot of bloat
Running OxygenOS 15.0, based on Android 15, the OnePlus Nord CE5 offers a pretty clean software experience with some seriously clever shortcuts built in. I like being able to swipe down with three fingers to take screenshots, while screen-off gestures that allow you to open the camera by tracing an O or switch on the flashlight by tracing a V are a fun touch. I can also see being able to lift the phone to my ear to auto-answer calls or flip it screen-down to mute them as features I’d end up using a lot.
On top of this, the Nord CE5 offers solid productivity features. For example, the smart sidebar allows you to quickly access your most-used apps by swiping from the top-right of the screen. Split View allows you to drag and drop two windows into a split-screen mode — not only does this feel super fluid to do, but you can easily resize each window by dragging the boundary between them.
It’s a little unfortunate then that OnePlus doesn’t seem able to resist the temptation to burden this otherwise lightweight experience with unnecessary bloat. Don’t get me wrong: it’s not the worst offender in this category. But the Nord CE5 still includes loads of apps that really should not be included by default, like AliExpress, Amazon Music or TikTok. Honestly, phone manufacturers: stop doing this.
The AI features on the Nord CE5 certainly aren’t as extreme as a phone like the Honor 600, with its Image to Video and wild VFX tools, but there are some useful tools available for tweaking your photos. Not only can you remove blur and reflections and upscale the quality of your images, but you can also erase those annoying people who walk straight through your shot and swap in a different expression for that one friend who always seems to have their eyes closed.
Overall, AI features are nicely unobtrusive, which is good news for those who are more AI-agnostic. The Google Gemini app comes pre-installed, offering answers, generative text and images. But if you’re not interested in its help, it’s easy to remove from your home and lockscreen, a pleasingly light-touch approach compared to some of the more gung-ho handsets.
Even if it doesn’t have the most cutting-edge advances, you can be sure the Nord CE5 will last you for the long haul. That’s because OnePlus has committed to providing six years of software support for its handset, something that’s definitely appreciated in an era when more of us are trying to eke more longevity out of our handsets, rather than ditch them every year.
All told, the software the Nord CE5 offers here isn’t groundbreaking. But it’s smooth and super-usable. Just please, OnePlus: shed some of that bloat.
- Software score: 4 / 5
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: performance
- Not the highest power chipset
- But productivity and gaming largely ran smoothly
- Very capable cooling
Given the OnePlus Nord CE5’s affordable price point, you won’t be surprised to hear that it doesn’t pack a top-of-the-range chipset. Don’t get me wrong: its MediaTek Dimensity 8350 Apex SoC isn’t bad, offering roughly similar performance to something like the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, but it doesn't offer as much thrust as many current flagship chips. With 8GB of RAM backing this up, I was expecting decent if unexceptional performance here.
And that’s generally what I found. During day-to-day productivity use, the Nord CE5 seems to run smoothly. Dipping in and out of apps, I never found any delays or witnessed anything hanging, no matter how many I opened. I even tried typing part of this review in split-screen mode while streaming What We Do In The Shadows — admittedly, this was atrocious for helping me focus, but both Google Docs and the video were unfaltering, marching on without a single misstep.
The Nord CE5 has surprisingly good gaming performance, given its budget price too. Playing Call of Duty: Mobile with the high-res texture packs, everything ran smoother than cappuccino foam. I played around eight ranked matches back-to-back and at no point did any judder or lag cause me to lose my kill-streak or stop me hoovering up MVP awards.
Genshin Impact was warier of the MediaTek Dimensity 8350 Apex chipset. While I was able to get balanced performance on the Higher graphics setting, switching it up to the Highest setting gave me a warning that I was overclocking the chipset. Despite this, the game still ran without any real issues — it’s possible the game developers were being overcautious, but I’ve obviously not conducted any long-term testing on how this might affect the life of the chip, so I’d urge caution before doing the same.
While some mid-range processors I’ve tested lately have gotten pretty warm during extended play sessions, I’m pleased to say that’s not an issue here. Thanks to its CryoVelocity graphene vapor chamber with a 7041mm² cooling area, the Nord CE5 stayed frosty even with Genshin Impact running at its overclocked settings. So while you might not get flagship-level performance out of the Nord CE5, it packs a pretty decent punch for such a low cost.
- Performance score: 4 / 5

OnePlus Nord CE5 review: camera
- Lush, vibrant colors
- Pro camera mode built-in
- Only offers 2x optical zoom
For the price, I was expecting the OnePlus Nord CE5’s camera to feel limited, but it’s actually relatively talented. First off, it’s capable of some bold, punchy HDR. One shot I snapped nearing the golden hour of a stone urn on a pedestal showed really deep blacks, while the highlights were warm enough to feel true-to-life.
Thanks to its 50MP resolution main lens, the OnePlus Nord CE5 is capable of crisp resolution, although its 1/1.95 inch sensor can't keep up with those offered by flagships. Zooming into a shot I took of a bumblebee crawling over a thistle, its detail was pleasingly crisp and kept everything wonderfully sharp. But, by comparison, my iPhone 16 Pro picked up every speck of pollen on its fuzzy coat in sharp detail and captured the sun reflected in its glossy black eye.
Colors are also captured with a real vibrance, the petals of a rose rendered in a wonderfully rich pink, for example. Naturally, you can’t expect top-tier chromatic performance here — my iPhone conveyed more range between darker and lighter tones and gave the dappling of each petal more pop. But the Nord CE5 still records delightfully lush hues and at least avoids the shortcut some brands take of oversaturating certain shades to artificially make images seem more vivid.
When taking photos close up, the OnePlus has a much shallower depth of field compared to some phones I’ve used. While that’s useful for creating a wonderful depth effect in your images, it does mean the Nord CE5 sometimes struggles to keep the whole subject in focus — some of the petals of a purple coneflower I shot looked slightly less crisp than on my iPhone, for example. Having said that, I actually quite like its bokeh, which feels much more Gaussian and subtle compared to phones that tend to make their bokeh too sharp and ‘swirly’.
While there are some decent Pro camera apps out there that unlock more granular control over your phone’s snapper, I love that OnePlus has already parceled this up in the Nord CE5’s native camera app. Using the Pro setting, I was able to tweak the camera’s ISO and shutter speed, as well as its white balance. For me though, the most invaluable setting is the manual lens’s focus, although this is far harder to set accurately on a phone screen than a DSLR viewfinder, so I do wish OnePlus had created a shortcut for zooming in on the screen while tweaking the focal range.
Night photography on the Nord CE5 is also generally strong. Taking shots at my favorite riverside pub at dusk, it struck a good balance between light and dark, with bright highlights not feeling overblown without compromising the shadows. Occasionally, faces could look a little soft around the edges, but that may have just been my subject not remaining as still as they could have. And at least the phone avoids overexposing night-time images — I’m not Truffaut, so I have no desire to shoot day for night or vice versa.
One area where I’d say the Nord CE5 falls further short of more premium phones is the zoom lenses. While the phone has a decent 2x optical zoom, it did make me realize how dependent I’ve become on my phone’s 5x optical zoom. On the plus side, the Nord CE5’s zoom lenses are crisp and distortion-free — the shots I snapped of flapping sky rats pigeons near a local river rendered their wings in decent detail.
All things considered, the Nord CE5’s camera is very good. Not only is using it an uncluttered experience, but its shots feel a lot truer to life than some of the flashier cams on other mid-market phones.
- Camera score: 4 / 5
OnePlus Nord CE5 review: battery
- Lengthy 20-hour battery life
- 80W charging fills battery in an hour
OnePlus generally packages outstanding batteries with its handsets, and the Nord CE5 is no exception. The brand suggests you should get several days of normal usage out of the CE5’s 5200mAh battery before needing to charge it.
Eager to put these claims to the test, I set the phone to stream a 2K video at 50% brightness on a loop — after 6 hours it had dropped to 71%, so I’d expect it to last roughly 20 hours and 40 minutes total. Not only does that mean OnePlus’s estimates are pretty on the money, but it also means the Nord CE5 comfortably outlasts many of the best phones on the market, whether premium options like the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra or budget bangers like Google Pixel 10a.
But where the OnePlus Nord CE5 really leaves all competition eating its dust is charging. Thanks to OnePlus’s 80W SUPERVOOC charging, topping up this handset feels faster than a pitstop fuel change — hooking it up to a cable and brick rated for up to 100W, it took around 59 minutes to go from 0% to 100%. While that’s not quite as ludicrous as the OnePlus 15’s blistering 120W charging, it still means you could juice it back up in the time it took you to scarf down your lunchtime bagel and boba tea.
So if your biggest priority in a budget phone is that it can last alongside you on your busiest days, the OnePlus Nord CE5 has definitely got you covered.
- Battery score: 5 / 5
Should I buy the OnePlus Nord CE5?

| Software | Smooth agile OS, great screen-off gestures and raise-to-answer functionality, solid productivity tools, discreet AI tools, six years of software support, annoying unnecessary bloatware. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | Chipset not top of the range but fares well, never witnessed any lag during productivity tasks and split-screening, games ran smoothly although running the highest graphics settings forced me to overclock the SoC, stayed cool during heavy loads. | 4 / 5 | 
| Cameras | Striking hues, strong contrast, good resolution that falls just a little short of flagships, surprisingly good low-light performance, soft subtle bokeh, only offers up to a 2x zoom. | 4 / 5 | 
| Battery life | Lengthy 20-hour battery, can charge from 0% to 100% in just 59 minutes. | 5 / 5 | 
| Value | While the Nord CE5 isn’t perfect, it offers quality that rivals many mid-market phones. And when you factor in its starting price of £299, that’s a whole heap of quality for not much cash. | 5 / 5 | 
Buy it if…
You need a battery that will go the distance
If you never want to get blindsided by an empty battery, the Nord CE5 has you covered. Not only should its 5,200mAh battery last you around 20 hours, but you can fully charge it in just one hour via its 80W SUPERVOOC.
You want a solid camera for a cheap price
Having tested a few mid-range phones whose cameras cut corners or overprocessed images, the Nord CE5’s camera is a breath of fresh air, focusing on getting the fundamentals right.
Don’t buy it if…
You’re after a top-tier gaming phone
If you like some casual gaming, the Nord CE5 will still deliver rock-solid stability. But if you want to play on the highest graphic settings, a higher-spec phone might be a better shout.
You want it to look bold even in daylight
Not only is the Nord CE5’s screen a little too shiny, it also can’t quite rival flagships when it comes to outdoor peak brightness. So if you want a phone that will outshine the midday sun, maybe look elsewhere.

RedMagic 10 Air
If you’re looking for a dedicated gaming phone, the RedMagic 10 Air sits right in that sweet spot between solid gaming performance and an affordable price. Costing $499 / £439 / AU$449, it offers the more powerful Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chipset, 12GB or 16GB of RAM and a more capacious 6,000mAh battery to help you get your game on. Read our full RedMagic 10 Air review.
OnePlus 15
Should you have a little more moolah to spend, the OnePlus 15 offers all the things that make the Nord CE5 great, dialed up to flagship levels. Its top-of-the-range Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset offers staggering performance, its stunningly detailed display is capable of a 450ppi pixel density and can hit refresh rates of 165Hz, while its battery is an enormous 7,300mAh. That’s a great spec given its price starts from $899.99 / £849 (around AU$1,290). Read our full OnePlus 15 review.
How I tested the OnePlus Nord CE5
- Used it over several weeks
- Tested a broad range of features
- Have spent more than 6 years covering phones
I tested the OnePlus Nord CE5 over the course of several weeks. To assess the performance of its display, I watched multiple HDR 4K videos and compared them side-by-side with my iPhone 16 Pro to assess contrast, color and brightness. I tried the camera out in a range of contexts, from shooting flowers with a short focal range to long-distance shots using the zoom.
When weighing up the performance of its chipset, I used the phone for a range of productivity tasks in split-screen mode and played a range of demanding games on their max graphics settings. Finally, to assess battery life, I set the phone to stream a 2K video at 50% brightness for six hours to assess how long it would take to drain the entire battery.
Having covered and reviewed gadgets for more than a decade, I have a lot of experience in this area and have tested a range of phones, tablets and drawing tablets during my time at TechRadar. I’m a keen smartphone photographer, having snapped over 47,000 photos over the last 15 years — a small proportion of which I’d say are actually competently shot — and a reformed smartphone game addict who still periodically falls off the wagon.

He’s an expert in a wide range of products from Spatial Audio headphones to gaming handhelds. When he’s not putting trailblazing tech through its paces, he can be found making melodic techno or seeking out the perfect cold brew coffee.

articles.title: Si se hace realidad, el proyecto Terafab de Elon Musk será la estructura interior más grande del planeta. Lo importante es el “si se hace realidad”
articles.text:
Si hay alguien que piense a lo grande hoy en día, ese es Elon Musk. El magnate es una personalidad absolutamente polarizadora que genera tanta admiración como críticas, pero no se le puede negar que su ambición sigue siendo espectacular. Su último proyecto, Terafab, es una colosal plata de fabricación de chips con una superficie total de unos 100 millones de pies cuadrados, unos 9,3 millones de metros cuadrados.
Tan grande que es mejor compararlo con otros megaedificios. Es una dimensión que es más fácil entender cuando uno ve lo pequeñitos que deja al Pentágono o al Apple Park. El divulgador Nic Cruz Patane comparaba precisamente las dimensiones de Terafab con esos edificios y otros como la planta Giga Texas (10 millones de pies cuadrados) o el Mall Of America (5,6 millones de pies cuadrados). El proyecto ocupa mucha más superficie que esas cuatro construcciones combinadas. Sobre el papel esta instalación sería un absoluto hito, pero como sucede con los megaproyectos de construcción de Arabia Saudí, del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho.
No será solo una fábrica gigantesca. SpaceX describe Terafab como un intento de integrar bajo una misma planta el diseño de las máscaras de fotolitografía, la fabricación de chips lógicos y de memoria, el empaquetado avanzado y las pruebas. Tesla necesita esos chips para sus vehículos y robots Optius, y SpaceX para su futura infraestructura de computación orbital. Intel se ha aliado con SpaceX para aportar toda su experiencia en este ámbito, y el objetivo que SpaceX a largo plazo es el de llegar a producir un teravatio de hardware de cómputo cada año.
Pero. La inversión inicial anunciada por SpaceX es de 16.800 millones de dólares, y el proyecto ya tiene ubicación clara: Grimes County, en Texas. En Reuters señalan que el presupuesto final podría ser mucho más elevado, porque la inversión total puede llegar a ser de 119.000 millones de dólares. La documentación de SpaceX es prudente, porque aunque existe una propuesta general, cada etapa se negociará por separado y tendrá sus propios plazos, inversiones y aprobación del consejo. Terafab no se construirá "de una vez".
El edificio puede ser fácil. Una gran planta de producción de automóviles ya es un proyecto descomunal, pero en el caso de destinarla a la producción de chips, los requisitos son aún más difíciles de escalar. Hay que crear salas limpias, suministro eléctrico continuo, tener disponibles grandes cantidades de agua pura y productos químicos, y desde luego acceso a una cadena de distribuidores entre los que ASML desempeña un papel insustituible. Musk ya ha hablado con la empresa holandesa y puede que SpaceX se acabe convirtiendo en uno de uss grandes clientes, pero una cosa está clara: tener superficie de terreno ya preparada no significa que pueda convertirse así como así en una planta de producción como la que plantean Tesla y SpaceX.
Aprender a fabricar chips de cero. Musk pretende aprovechar el futuro proceso de fabricación 14A de Intel, una tecnología con la que la empresa estadounidense quiere recortar terreno con TSMC. Eso significa que Terafab no solo dependerá de sí misma, sino también de que Intel logre que esa tecnología funcione de forma competitiva y con buenos rendimientos (yields). Hay aún importantes incógnitas sobre la financiación y el calendario, pero es que aprender a fabricar chips de cero es otro reto igual de colosal que la propia dimensión de la compañía.
Pero todo se ha puesto en marcha. Lo cierto es que Terafab ya cuenta con una inversión inicial comprometida, obras de preparación en Teas y los acuerdos de Tesla, SpaceX e Intel firmados, además de conversaciones con socios tecnológicos. Así pues, esto no es solo un tuit de Elon Musk en X, sino una iniciativa que comienza a andar. Los obstáculos son desde luego extraordinarios, pero como mínimo habría que concederle el beneficio de la duda a este magnate, que ya desafió la industria aeroespacial y la del automóvil para revolucionarlas completamente.
Si se hace realidad. Elon Musk lleva años intentando resolver los cuellos de botella de sus empresas con una estrategia ya aplicada por otros: controlar cada vez más partes de la cadena. Cohetes, satélites, baterías, centros de datos, generación eléctrica... Terafab lleva esa filosofía a la complejísima industria de los semiconductores, y si alcanza la dimensión anunciada, convertiría a Tesla y SpaceX en referente absoluto para la fabricación de microchips.

articles.title: Cutting RAG inference costs 6x starts with deciding what never reaches the LLM
articles.text: Most teams building retrieval augmented generation (RAG) systems for high stakes classification make the same architectural bet: Route every ambiguous case straight to the language model and trust the retrieved context to sort it out. This works fine in a demo. It falls apart the moment the system has to survive an audit, a regulator, or a compliance officer asking why a specific decision was made six months ago. I have spent the last year building RAG based classification systems in regulated enterprise settings, where the cost of a wrong answer is not a bad chatbot reply. A decision has to hold up to scrutiny long after the model produced it. This environment forces a different design philosophy than most AI engineering content assumes. Here is what changes when you cannot afford to be probabilistic about everything, and how a cascade architecture solves it. The invisible cost of an all LLM pipeline The appeal of routing everything through a large language model (LLM) is obvious: Fewer moving parts, faster iteration, the model handles unanticipated edge cases. The problem shows up later, in three places. First, auditability. "The model decided based on retrieved context" is not an acceptable answer. You need a decision path a human can reconstruct without rerunning inference and hoping for the same output. Second, cost at scale. If your system processes tens of thousands of cases a day and every one hits an LLM call with several retrieved documents in context, your inference bill and latency both scale with volume in a way that rule based logic does not. Third, and least discussed, model drift on the easy cases. LLMs are excellent at nuanced judgment calls. They are inconsistent, in ways that are hard to detect, on cases that should have a deterministic answer. A clear structured match against known criteria should never depend on a language model's mood. The cascade approach The fix: Stop treating the LLM as the front line and start treating it as the escalation path. In practice this means a three stage pipeline. Stage one is deterministic. Exact matches, structured field comparisons, and anything with a clear rule get resolved here with no model call at all. This stage should clear the majority of volume, often more than half depending on your data quality, and every decision is fully explainable because it is a lookup, not an inference. Stage two is where retrieval earns its keep. For cases that survive stage one — and I mean survive as in they were not clearly resolved — you build a retrieval layer that pulls the specific evidence relevant to the ambiguity: Prior reviewer decisions on similar cases, contextual documents that explain an apparent conflict, or historical precedent that clarifies an edge case. The retrieval step matters more than the generation step here. If you retrieve the wrong context, even the best language model in the world will produce a confident, well reasoned, wrong answer. Stage three is the LLM call , and it should only see the residue that stages one and two could not resolve. This is the part people skip when they design their first version, and it is the single biggest lever for both cost and quality. In one system I worked on, routing only the genuinely ambiguous 10 to 15% of cases to the LLM cut inference cost by roughly 6X compared to an all LLM baseline, while improving consistency on the deterministic majority to effectively perfect. Designing the prompt for asymmetric risk Once a case reaches the LLM stage, most teams default to a neutral prompt: "Assess whether this case should be approved or flagged." That framing is wrong for high stakes classification because the cost of the two error types is not symmetric. Missing something that genuinely needed attention can mean real harm downstream. Incorrectly flagging something that was fine costs a reviewer's time and a delay. Those two outcomes are rarely equally bad, yet a neutral prompt asks the model to treat them as if they were. An asymmetric risk prompt makes that tradeoff explicit to the model rather than letting it guess at your risk tolerance. Concretely, this means instructing the model to treat uncertainty as a reason to escalate rather than clear, providing calibrated examples of both error types with their consequences spelled out, and asking for a confidence score alongside the classification rather than a binary answer. The confidence score becomes your second cascade point: Anything below a certain threshold goes to a human reviewer instead of being auto resolved, no matter what the model's classification says. This sounds like a small prompt engineering detail. In practice it is the difference between a system that reduces reviewer workload and one that quietly increases risk while looking like it is working. Evaluating a system like this properly Standard RAG evaluation metrics were not built with this use case in mind, and using them without adaptation will give you a false sense of confidence. A few adjustments that matter. Retrieval quality needs to be measured separately from final classification accuracy. A system can have excellent retrieval ranking scores and still make bad final decisions if the generation step misweights the evidence. Track them independently. Your evaluation set needs deliberate oversampling of the cases that reach stage three, since that is where your system's judgment actually gets tested. If your eval set mirrors your production distribution, it will be dominated by the deterministic cases your cascade already handles well, and you will be blind to exactly the failures that matter most. LLM as judge evaluation works for this domain but only if the judge prompt encodes the same asymmetric risk framing as your production prompt. A judge that treats both error types equally will systematically favor the wrong tradeoff when you are tuning your system. Finally, build a feedback loop from confirmed outcomes back into your retrieval corpus. When a human reviewer overturns a model decision, that case and its correct resolution should become retrievable context for future similar cases. Without this, your system's handling of ambiguous cases never improves, it just keeps making the same category of mistake at the same rate. The broader lesson The instinct to reach for the most capable model for every decision is understandable, but in domains where wrong answers have real consequences, the more valuable engineering work is deciding what should never touch the model at all. Cascade architecture is not a workaround for LLM limitations. It is what a mature RAG system looks like once you have actually had to defend its decisions to someone whose job is to find the flaw in your logic. If you are building AI systems for any regulated or high stakes domain, the question worth asking before you write a single prompt is not "How do I get the model to handle this well." It is "Which parts of this decision should never have been the model's job in the first place." Vineet Vijay is a Lead AI and machine learning engineer.

articles.title: This portable, external CD/DVD drive comes with a 2.5-inch SATA and an SD Card slot for just $26 — Save 10% on a modern essential for keeping physical media alive
articles.text:
This portable, external CD/DVD drive comes with a 2.5-inch SATA and an SD Card slot for just $26 — Save 10% on a modern essential for keeping physical media alive
Plug-and-play convenience matches utility.
As the AI boom consumes everything tangible around us, it's even more important to keep physical media alive. Since our current tech isn't equipped to interface with these relics, an external disc drive is a great investment to access your collection. Alronly makes a great CD/DVD player that also comes with a 2.5-inch SATA and SD Card slot, along with standard USB ports, for just $26.99 on Amazon.
Alrony's Portable USB device does CD reading and writing at up to 24X, and DVD reading and writing at up to 8X, 2.5-inch SATA drive docking, as well as providing easy-reach slots for full-size SD cards, microSD cards, 2x USB-A ports, and a USB-C.
This drive is absolutely packed with features for the price. It can read and write CDs at a blazing-fast 24X, or at 8X speeds for DVD. It also acts as a USB hub and a SATA-to-USB adapter. You can use the 2.5-inch SATA slot for either a hard drive or an SSD. It provides easy-to-reach access to a full-size SD card slot, microSD slot, 2x USB-A ports, and USB-C — both of those are promised to be USB 3.0 with 5 Gbps speeds.
Alrony says this USB attached device is compatible with Windows XP, 7, 8, and 10, as well as a wide gamut of Linux and MacOS computers. It's a true plug-and-play device that doesn't require downloading any drivers, making it very suitable for older family members that consider you tech support. Just don’t expect to use it with your iOS, Android, or ChromeOS device; they are specifically stated to be incompatible.
The include cable for data/power has both a USB-A and USB-C connector. Meanwhile, the drive also includes another USB-C port for dedicated power, which may be useful in case your chosen system’s data port is not up to scratch in power delivery terms. The device is also quite sleek, measuring just 0.9 inches thick and weighing only 0.75 pounds with an all-black aesthetic that would fit basically anywhere.
While CDs and DVDs don't hold a candle to Blu-Ray, the best physical media standard we have today, they still hold an important place in history. Even if you don't have any special memories stored in old discs, you can use this external drive to put new ones on there. For just $26.99, this is a great tool to have by your desktop that can still be put to good use when it's not reading or writing to optical media.

articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro : les 10 nouveautés majeures prévues par Apple
articles.text:
iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro : les 10 nouveautés majeures prévues par Apple
Vous hésitez entre passer à l’iPhone 18 Pro ou au 18 Pro Max et opter pour les iPhone 17 Pro ? On fait le point sur les nouveautés attendues sur cette future génération de smartphones Apple.
Attendus pour le mois prochain, les iPhone 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max n’ont déjà plus de secrets. Les rumeurs ont en effet craché le morceau depuis le lancement des iPhone 17 Pro, nous permettant ainsi de dresser le tableau des 10 grosses nouveautés à venir sur cette nouvelle génération. L’une d’entre elles n’est cependant pas du tout bonne à prendre.
Un design repensé en 3 points pour les iPhone 18 Pro
Au niveau du design, Apple aurait trois évolutions clés au programme pour démarquer les iPhone 18 Pro du modèle actuel. La plus visible se passerait logiquement du côté des coloris. Après le très populaire Orange cosmique des iPhone 17 Pro, la nouvelle star de 2026 opterait pour un rouge bordeaux séduisant, nommé “Dark Cherry”.
Apple opterait aussi pour le retour d’une teinte bleu clair, tout en conservant le traditionnel gris. Il se pourrait même que le noir fasse son grand retour, sous la dénomination “Dark Grey” (gris sombre). En bref, cette génération aurait de quoi satisfaire tout autant les personnes ayant besoin de sobriété que celles voulant se démarquer et accueillir la couleur dans leur vie.
Ces nouvelles teintes viendraient aussi avec un remaniement de la surface du dos. Le châssis en aluminium et la zone MagSafe en verre auraient une apparence bi-ton beaucoup moins prononcée que sur les iPhone 17 Pro. Cela offrirait ainsi un design bien plus unifié entre ces deux zones.
Le troisième changement marquant au niveau de l’apparence des iPhone 18 Pro se situe au niveau de l’écran, avec enfin du changement pour la Dynamic Island. Introduite avec les iPhone 14 Pro, cette zone évoluerait enfin pour gagner en finesse. D’après les rumeurs, Apple aurait opté pour une version 35 % plus petite. En plus d’agrandir la surface d’affichage de la dalle, cela offrirait aussi un espace parfait pour rendre toute sa rondeur au nouveau Siri boosté à l’IA d’iOS 27.
Toujours plus de puissance et de connectivité, le secret des puces A20 Pro et Apple C2
À l’intérieur des iPhone 18 Pro, on retrouverait l’A20 Pro, première puce Apple gravée en 2 nanomètres contre 3 auparavant. Une finesse qui a tout son sens, étant donné qu’elle offrirait un gain de vitesse de 15 % et une consommation énergétique réduite de 30 % face à l’A19 Pro des iPhone 17 Pro. Elle intégrerait au passage pour la première fois la mémoire vive en son sein, un coup de boost non négligeable pour Apple Intelligence et le traitement des données sur iPhone.
La seconde grosse évolution viendrait du modem 5G maison utilisé sur cette génération : l’Apple C2. Succédant aux très réussis C1 et C1X, il offrirait pour la première fois à l’iPhone la possibilité de se connecter à Internet avec le réseau satellitaire. Un avantage non négligeable pour rester connecté en tout temps, même dans les zones blanches, soit celles où le réseau mobile n’est pas accessible.
Cela permettrait par exemple de s’orienter lors d’une randonnée isolée en montagne, d’échanger des messages ou de passer des appels via des applications de messagerie tierces en haute mer ou encore de rester connecté en cas de panne.
Une autonomie revue à la hausse sur iPhone 18 Pro
En plus de tirer parti de l’efficacité énergétique de la puce A20 Pro, les iPhone 18 Pro devraient gagner en autonomie grâce à deux autres changements majeurs.
Le premier est le plus évident : de plus grandes batteries. Alors que la variante Pro gagnerait seulement 1 % de capacité en plus, le modèle Pro Max profiterait d’une révolution importante en passant à 5 567 mAh aux États-Unis (version eSIM-only), contre 5 391 mAh pour le reste du monde adoptant encore l’emplacement pour carte SIM (dont la France).
Bien qu’on puisse être déçu sur le Vieux Continent, sachez qu’on est tout de même face à un gain de 10 % de batterie, ce qui pourrait nous permettre de tenir quelques heures supplémentaires sans avoir à passer par la case recharge. Une telle augmentation de capacité signerait aussi un peu d’embonpoint supplémentaire par rapport à l’épaisseur de l’iPhone 17 Pro Max.
À cela s’ajouterait un nouvel écran adoptant la technologie LTPO+, optimisant la consommation énergétique de la dalle tout au long de la journée. De quoi limiter son impact sur l’autonomie sans rien faire. Cette nouveauté signerait aussi une meilleure gestion de la luminosité par les iPhone 18 Pro, atténuant avec elle certaines distorsions disgracieuses (comme les scintillements à basse luminosité ou encore les dérives colorimétriques).
Du nouveau pour le capteur photo principal et la caméra selfie
Côté photographie, le module photo arrière miserait sur une nouveauté majeure : un capteur principal avec ouverture variable. Une avancée technique qui offrirait aux utilisateurs un contrôle bien plus précis sur l’exposition et la profondeur de champ. En modifiant physiquement l’ouverture du diaphragme, l’iPhone 18 Pro pourrait réguler la quantité de lumière atteignant le capteur, limitant ainsi la surexposition en plein soleil tout en optimisant le piqué.
Les photographes en herbe profiteraient également d’un flou d’arrière-plan (bokeh) naturel, sans dépendre uniquement des algorithmes logiciels, pour un rendu plus authentique et professionnel.
À l’avant, la caméra frontale monterait une nouvelle fois en gamme avec l’intégration d’un capteur de 24 Mpx, succédant à la récente optique de 18 Mpx introduite sur les iPhone 17. Un gain de 6 Mpx bienvenu, pour des photos plus nettes et riches en détails, tout en améliorant le rendu lors des appels vidéo. Ce surcroît de définition offrirait également plus de marge pour le recadrage et le suivi automatique du visage pour la fonction Center Stage.
Un prix clairement revu à la hausse pour les iPhone 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max
Après les bonnes nouvelles, les nouveautés, passons à la grosse mauvaise nouvelle : le prix des iPhone 18 Pro. Aux dernières nouvelles, on apprenait que le coût des composants de cette génération serait 38 % plus élevé par rapport à ce qu’Apple payait pour les iPhone 17 Pro.
Les divers informateurs parlent effectivement d’une hausse généralisée de 200 à 300 $, ce qui pourrait se matérialiser par une hausse allant de 330 à 440 € en France. Le prix de départ de l’iPhone 18 Pro serait fixé à 1 399 $, faisant ainsi débuter la gamme premium d’Apple de 2026 à environ 1 659 € en France au lieu de 1 329 €.
Tout cela s’explique par une situation dont on entend parler depuis de nombreux mois : la pénurie de mémoire, causée par les besoins colossaux de ces ressources pour l’infrastructure IA. En plus d’impacter le coût de la RAM et du stockage, cela se répercute peu à peu sur le reste, et en particulier sur les processeurs.
En bref : Apple doit absolument répercuter cela sur le prix de vente final des iPhone 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max, histoire de se garantir un volume de ventes suffisant sans braquer ses clients.
Pour information, le nombre de modèles au lancement serait limité à cause de la pénurie de RAM, avec un milliard de dollars d’A20 Pro attendant impatiemment d’intégrer la mémoire vive en leur sein, et donc de finaliser l’assemblage des prochains smartphones d’Apple.

articles.title: Rentrée : ces iPhone dernière génération passent à 20 € par mois sans intérêt

Renouveler son smartphone à la rentrée revient souvent à sortir plus de mille euros d’un coup. Bouygues Telecom prend le problème par un autre bout et découpe la facture sur trois ans, forfait 5G compris.
La dernière génération d’iPhone est disponible chez Bouygues Telecom avec une formule de financement étalée dans le temps. Le principe : un premier versement de 49 € au moment de l’achat, puis des mensualités fixes pendant 36 mois, à partir de 20 € par mois. L’ensemble s’articule autour du Forfait Intégral 250 Go, facturé 29,99 € par mois la première année au lieu de 34,99 €, puis 39,99 € par mois, avec un engagement de 24 mois sur la ligne.
Trois leviers s’ajoutent à ce socle et pèsent sur la facture finale : la reprise de votre ancien mobile déclenche un bonus différé, le code BOOST100 retire 100 € immédiatement sur l’iPhone 17 Pro associé aux forfaits Intégral et Intégral+, et le paiement Smart Change autorise un changement d’appareil tous les 12 mois.
Pourquoi financer son iPhone sur 36 mois plutôt qu’en une fois ?
Le paiement échelonné répond d’abord à une contrainte de trésorerie : il supprime le pic de dépense au moment de l’achat et le remplace par une ligne budgétaire stable. Le crédit étant proposé à taux 0 %, le montant total remboursé correspond au prix du téléphone, sans surcoût.
L’autre intérêt tient au couplage avec le forfait. Une enveloppe de 250 Go en 5G absorbe sans difficulté le streaming vidéo, les réseaux sociaux, le GPS et le partage de connexion en télétravail. Combinée à la reprise mobile, cette architecture agit sur le coût total de possession plutôt que sur le seul prix du terminal.

I'm an Apple Watch die-hard — here are my picks for the 10 best Apple Watch faces of 2026 so far
Apple has some awesome Watch faces – here are my top picks
Apple makes some of the best smartwatches you can buy in 2026, especially if you're already an existing iPhone or MacBook user and embedded in Apple's ecosystem.
In many ways, the Apple Watch is Apple's most personal device, sitting right on your wrist, with plenty of color and band options – not to mention loads of different watch faces to pick from. The face you pick is where the fun really starts, as it can make the same watch feel sporty, traditional, playful, or completely different from one day to the next.
I tend to favour simpler, less complicated faces that make the time easy to read without cramming the screen with data, all of which is still available inside various apps. But I've included all sorts here. From my daily-driver Flux face to Snoopy’s wonderfully unpredictable animations, these are the 10 Apple Watch faces I’d recommend trying in 2026.
What's your favorite watch face? Let us know in the comments below!
Infograph – best Apple Watch face for complications
Infograph is the obvious pick for anyone who wants plenty of information on-screen. It supports up to eight complications, although I prefer a cleaner setup with just four fitness-focused ones in the centre.
Why it works: You can tailor it around work, exercise, weather, or everyday shortcuts, and most complications open the relevant app when tapped. Leaving a few spaces empty also makes it much easier to read at a glance.
Limitations: It can become cluttered very quickly, especially once you start mixing lots of colors and data types. If you mainly want to check the time, Infograph is probably more watch face than you need.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Flow – best Liquid Glass Apple Watch face
Flow is one of the clearest showcases for watchOS 26’s Liquid Glass design, with oversized translucent numerals set against a colorful animated background. You can switch between different colors, two typefaces, and a static or moving backdrop.
Why it works: The large numbers are easy to read, while the refraction effect gives the face much more depth when you move your wrist. Blue and purple suits the glassy look particularly well, but brighter combinations can make it feel completely different.
Limitations: There are no complications, so Flow is firmly a design-first face. Its glossy, futuristic style is also probably too bold for anyone who wants their Apple Watch to resemble a traditional watch.
California – best traditional Apple Watch face
California is the closest this list gets to a classic watch dial, mixing Roman and Arabic numerals in its most recognisable form. You can also switch between several numeral styles, use a circular or full-screen layout, and add a handful of complications.
Why it works: It gives the Apple Watch a more traditional look without losing useful extras such as the date, weather, or app shortcuts. Darker colors and restrained complications suit it especially well.
Limitations: Bright or overly detailed complications can clash with the clean dial, while the full-screen version leaves less room for information. It's also less playful than Apple’s more modern faces.
Numerals Duo – best bold digital Apple Watch face
Numerals Duo fills almost the entire screen with oversized hours and minutes, like Flow, making it one of Apple’s easiest faces to read at a glance. You can change the colors, numeral system, and choose between Filled, Hybrid, and Outline styles.
Why it works: The huge numbers give it some personality without making the time difficult to find. My multi-colored Hybrid version is especially playful, but a simpler two-color setup can look much cleaner.
Limitations: There are no complications, so you lose quick access to weather, fitness data, and so on. It is also unapologetically digital, which may not appeal if you prefer a more watch-like design.
Snoopy – best character Apple Watch face
Snoopy brings the Apple Watch to life with short animations featuring Snoopy, Woodstock, and the clock hands. The scenes change throughout the day, while different color options give the face a slightly different feel.
Why it works: The animations are really charming and varied enough to stay fun beyond the first few days. My “ARF!” scene pictured above captures the playful side of the face particularly well.
Limitations: There are no complications, and some animations briefly make the time harder to read. The Snoopy face might work best as a weekend-only option.
Flux – best dynamic digital Apple Watch face
Flux is my daily-driver face, combining oversized numerals with a block of color that rises from the bottom as each minute passes. You can switch between different colors and Western Arabic, Eastern Arabic, or Devanagari numerals.
Why it works: It is simple, bold, and immediately readable, but the constant movement stops it from feeling static. The numerals also shift into a new shape whenever the minute changes. Really cool face.
Limitations: Flux has no complications, so it only tells you the time. The unusual numeral shapes can also take a little getting used to, particularly with some color combinations.
Color – best minimalist analogue Apple Watch face
Color is a clean, flexible analogue face that can be dressed up with bright shades or kept deliberately understated. You can choose between circular and dial layouts, including a full-screen version, and then add complications or a monogram.
Why it works: It keeps the focus on the time while still leaving room for a useful shortcut or two. My full-screen version uses a single Camera Remote complication, but the circular layout can carry much more information.
Limitations: It lacks the personality of Apple’s more animated faces, and adding too many complications quickly undermines its simplicity.
Timelapse – best scenic Apple Watch face
Timelapse turns your watch into a tiny moving cityscape, with options including London, New York City, Paris, Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Mack Lake. My pick is the London version, because it's where I live, complete with Westminster and a small weather complication.
Why it works: The shifting background gives it more atmosphere than a static photo face, while the time stays easy to spot. It also feels a little more personal when you choose a location you know.
Limitations: The selection of scenes is quite limited, and readability can vary depending on the frame. There is also likely to be a higher battery drain, and it offers far less customisation than Apple’s Photos face.
Artist – best art-led Apple Watch face
Finally, Artist turns the screen into a tiny changing portrait, with the time worked directly into the illustration. Tapping the face produces a new combination, so it rarely looks exactly the same twice.
Why it works: It feels more like a small piece of digital art than a traditional watch face. The shifting faces and colors give it plenty of personality without relying on animation. A slightly offbeat, cool pick.
Limitations: There are no complications, and some combinations are easier to read than others. It is also the least practical option here if you mainly use your watch as an information hub.
How to add and customise Apple Watch faces
The easiest method is through the Watch app on your iPhone.
Open the Face Gallery, choose a design, then adjust its colors, style, numerals, and complications before tapping Add to Watch.
The available controls vary a lot: Flow mainly offers visual tweaks, while Infograph lets you change almost every piece of information on-screen, and so on.
You can also make changes directly on the watch. Touch and hold the current face, tap Edit, then swipe through the available options and turn the Digital Crown to make your selections.
How to pick the right Apple Watch face
The best place to start is with what you actually want to see when you raise your wrist. That might be nothing more than the time, or it could include your next appointment, Activity rings, weather, and a shortcut to your most-used app.
Complications are useful, but from experience, more is not always better. Too much information can make things feel cluttered, especially if you have a smaller model like my Apple Watch SE.
It's also worth setting up a few faces for different situations. You might use Infograph during the working day, switch to something fitness-focused for a workout, then move to Snoopy at the weekend.
Finally, test each face outdoors and at a quick glance – a color combination that looks great in the Watch app may be much harder to read on your wrist.

articles.title: Anthropic multiplica ingresos por 14 y prepara su OPV antes que OpenAI
articles.text:
Anthropic, la empresa de inteligencia artificial responsable del chatbot Claude, ha registrado un crecimiento exponencial en sus ingresos y se prepara para debutar en bolsa antes que su principal rival, OpenAI.
Según documentos filtrados y reportes de Bloomberg News, los ingresos del segundo trimestre de Anthropic se multiplicaron por 14 frente al mismo periodo del año anterior, superando los US$11.500 millones. Este salto sitúa a la compañía como uno de los grandes protagonistas de la carrera global por la inteligencia artificial.
PUBLICIDAD
El contexto es de máxima competencia. Mientras Anthropic acelera sus planes de salida a bolsa, OpenAI también ha iniciado trámites confidenciales ante la SEC, pero su debut podría retrasarse.
Crecimiento récord y previsiones de ingresos
En el último año, Anthropic ha escalado posiciones gracias a la adopción masiva de su tecnología por parte de clientes corporativos y desarrolladores. Su tasa anualizada de ingresos superó los US$47.000 millones en mayo, y los inversores proyectan que esa cifra podría alcanzar entre US$100.000 y US$120.000 millones a finales de 2026. De confirmarse, la compañía multiplicaría por diez sus ingresos en menos de dos años.
PUBLICIDAD
En comparación, OpenAI mantiene una tasa anual cercana a los US$40.000 millones, aunque los métodos de cálculo pueden variar entre ambas firmas.
Así será la OPV de Anthropic: bancos, valoración y calendario
Anthropic ha presentado de manera confidencial su documentación ante la SEC y colabora con Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs y JPMorgan Chase para estructurar su oferta pública inicial. La valoración estimada para el debut supera los US$2 billones (1,7 billones de euros), lo que convertiría la operación en la mayor OPV de la historia, superando incluso el récord alcanzado por SpaceX.
PUBLICIDAD
Las fuentes citadas por Financial Times y The Wall Street Journal anticipan que el debut bursátil podría producirse entre finales de septiembre y principios de octubre. El objetivo es aprovechar el apetito de los mercados por empresas tecnológicas y mantener la ventaja frente a OpenAI y otros competidores como DeepSeek, la firma china que también prepara su salto al parqué.
Rondas de inversión y valoración de Anthropic
El crecimiento de Anthropic ha ido acompañado de rondas de financiación millonarias, con inversiones lideradas por fondos como Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Greenoaks y Sequoia Capital. En mayo, la compañía levantó US$65.000 millones, superando una valoración previa de US$965.000 millones. Solo unos meses antes, en febrero, había captado US$30.000 millones, consolidándose como la startup de IA más valiosa del mundo en ese momento.
PUBLICIDAD
Estos recursos han permitido a Anthropic acelerar el desarrollo de modelos avanzados y cerrar acuerdos estratégicos, como el pacto de US$10.000 millones con una startup de computación en la nube para ampliar infraestructura y servicios.
Competencia directa con OpenAI y el ecosistema de IA
La rivalidad entre Anthropic y OpenAI es el motor de una carrera que involucra cientos de miles de millones de dólares en inversión global. Ambas empresas buscan captar clientes corporativos y desarrollar los modelos más avanzados, pero Anthropic se ha adelantado al presentar primero sus trámites de OPV y buscar el respaldo del mercado público.
PUBLICIDAD
La competencia también se da en la captación de talento, la adquisición de startups (como el interés de Anthropic en Decart) y la consolidación de alianzas con grandes tecnológicas y fondos soberanos internacionales.
El mercado de salidas a bolsa vive un renacimiento: en lo que va de año, las OPV han recaudado más de US$256.400 millones, la mayor cifra desde 2021. El interés por la inteligencia artificial y la expectativa de nuevas aplicaciones han dinamizado la inversión y puesto a empresas como Anthropic en el centro de la escena financiera.
PUBLICIDAD
Si Anthropic logra debutar en Wall Street antes que OpenAI y DeepSeek, marcaría un hito en el sector de la inteligencia artificial y fijaría un punto de referencia para futuras OPV tecnológicas. El crecimiento de los ingresos, la escalada en valoración y la anticipación de los inversores aseguran que la salida al parqué de Anthropic será uno de los eventos más seguidos del año.
